newsitem.title: UK: VLCC spot rates forecast to dip before rising again.
newsitem.headline: VLCC spot rates forecast to dip before rising again.

text.p: Spot market rates of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) are forecast to dip over the next three months before rising again in the autumn, according to a London shipping analyst.
Maritime Strategies International (MSI) said in its report for March that spot rates would decline as seasonal demand subsided.

"The market will come under pressure as vessels start to return to loading areas. However, in line with events in 1995/96 rates will start to recover by mid-year as third quarter 1997 stock building gets under way," MSI said.
The report added that the time charter market would become interesting over the next six months and advised that owners would be well advised to target Middle Eastern charterers.
MSA forecast spot rates for 270,000dwt vessels Gulf-Europe slipping from February's average $17,000 a day to $15,500 around June before rising to around $21,000 by August.
Gulf-East rates would slip off $21,300 to $20,500 before increasing again to $29,000 over the same period, MSI predicted.
Suezmax spot rates were predicted to decrease slowly over the next few months from averages of $23,300 a day in February to $21,500 a day by August.

MSI predicted that Iraqi Ceyhan exports would remain the major stimulant to the Mediterranean market, in turn benefiting the Atlantic trades by accelerating the migration of older tonnage into Med trading.
The report added that Aframax spot rates would rise slightly before falling again.

"MSI anticipates that average earnings will fall below $20,000 a day over the next six months, although they will remain above 1996 levels and there is the potential for rate spikes during the period," it said.
For 30,000dwt product rates, MSI said: "Earnings will fall steadily over the next quarter before stabilising at over $12,500 a day in the third quarter of 1997."

However, it added that the market would benefit from the completion of U.S. refinery maintenance programmes, which peaked in February, and below average refinery outages in Europe and Japan forecast for the second quarter.
